bull_bear.title: Capital allocation

bull_bear.body:
- Order-inflow guidance reliability (missed FY26 by ~28%; BESS cancellation). Verify FY27 INR 12,000 cr inflow tracking.
- MDO ramp risk — guidance already cut; CCL washery dependency, monsoon seasonality, single-month (March) revenue spike not sustainable run-rate.
- Water division receivable/certification overhang (central-govt fund release dependent).
- Labor availability (40,000+ headcount, 70–75% labor; civil labor from WB/Odisha/Jharkhand/UP) and attrition.
- BHEL packaging-philosophy change could pressure pricing/qualification on installation orders.
- Commodity inflation on fixed-price portions not covered by PVC.
bull_bear.title: Risks & watch-items

bull_bear.body: Confident, bullish, granular on numbers — CFO gave specific mine economics, margin bridges, and candidly acknowledged the order-inflow miss and the MDO guidance cut (conservative framing). Transparent on water-division drag. Tone credible; repeatedly emphasized power-sector visibility to FY30 and O&M-led margin improvement.
bull_bear.title: Management quality / tone

bull_bear.body:
- The MDO FY28 guidance was quietly cut ~35% (INR ~1,850 cr → INR 1,250 cr) vs the Feb-26 call — a key negative not flagged in the opening remarks.
- March-26 MDO revenue (INR 117 cr) was an exceptional client-driven offtake spike; normalized run-rate is INR 40–50 cr/month — investors extrapolating Q4 MDO (INR 226 cr) would overstate FY27.
- "EPC" segment now replaces the discontinued Transmission/Electricals division; railway work folded into civil — segment-label change, not pure new growth.
- The thermal thesis is explicitly a renewable-integration play: management argues 150→300GW solar creates grid imbalance requiring more thermal for night/day-night operation — a contrarian-sounding but coherent grid-stability argument.
- Receivables-driven OCF jump (74 lakh → 430 cr) is the single biggest balance-sheet positive and underappreciated vs the headline order-miss narrative.
bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Operation and maintenance franchise described by the Chairman as already the largest in the country, with about 36,246 MW under contract of which roughly 7,541 MW sits under comprehensive contracts governed by key performance indicators and about 14,380 MW under semi-comprehensive contracts
- Annuity depth and customer concentration in the private sector: long-term contracts cover 29,296 MW across 20 plants in the private sector and 6,950 MW across six plants in the government sector
- Workforce scale behind the annuity business, with about 18,000 people across skill sets including around 3,600 engineers and supervisors, plus maintenance management and diagnostic systems and in-house training facilities
- Ability to take the full scope on the mechanical island rather than individual packages, at a time when owners are paying for schedule certainty and a single accountable party
- Qualification credential established by the Singareni Stage-II award: balance of plant on EPC basis for an 800 MW unit is the qualification threshold most state and central tenders apply, and the mandate establishes that credential
- Ability to coordinate civil and mechanical scope together, which matters because civil work is the pacing item on a power project and foundation-to-commissioning readiness governs when boiler and turbine erection can begin
- In-house fabrication shop supporting work executed during live plant shutdowns, where speed rather than scale is the constraint
- Entry into nuclear via civil works for the 1,400 MW Kaiga project awarded in FY 2024-25, building experience of the quality and safety regime that segment requires
- Established international base entered in 2000 with the first overseas office opened in Dubai in 2013, over 1,500 specialists and skilled workers deployed, and a portfolio shifting from manpower deployment towards performance-linked contracts that are renewable and lower working capital
- Order backlog including long-tenure mining contracts closed the year at Rs 55,151 Cr, giving multi-year visibility
- Diversification discipline stated by the Chairman: the Company enters a vertical only when it draws on a capability it already holds
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Client concentration — A significant share of revenue is drawn from a limited number of large clients and government entities, so a material reduction in their capital programmes would affect revenue disproportionately. Listed both as a Threat and in the risk management table; mitigation is to broaden the client base across private enterprises and new sectors and to lengthen contract tenors so revenue is less dependent on annual award cycles.
- Delays in government fund allocation holding up certification and collection — Receivables can remain outstanding where budgetary allocation to a government-funded programme is delayed, holding up certification and collection. The AR states this has been a feature of the water business during the year, and the Chairman attributes margin pressure in the water division to certification of completed work by the state remaining delayed through the year.
- Competitive intensity and margin compression — The construction and maintenance sector has a large number of participants of varying scale, domestic and international, offering comparable services; this can intensify competition, compress margins and lower the probability of conversion on competitively bid work. Mitigation is long-term client relationships, specialised services where the field is narrower, and selective bidding rather than bidding on volume.
- Input cost and supply chain exposure on fixed-price work — Prices of steel, cement and other inputs fluctuate and delivery of manufactured items can slip, with geopolitical disruption able to move prices sharply, giving higher project cost and margin erosion on fixed-price work. Mitigation is contracts incorporating price adjustment clauses, long-term supply arrangements and hedging where instruments are available.
- Execution and site-access risk — Weather, site access, land availability and clearance delays can disrupt execution, producing schedule slippage, cost escalation and exposure to liquidated damages. Mitigation is planning with contingency, project controls and scheduling systems, and holding safety and quality standards across sites.
- Safety and reputational exposure on heavy-machinery and live-plant work — Heavy machinery, working at height and live plant environments carry inherent safety risk; an incident or compliance failure can give rise to injury, legal consequence, contractual penalty and reputational damage. Mitigation is safety management systems, training and audit at every site, with incident reporting and corrective action tracked to closure.
- International operations: political, currency and jurisdictional exposure — Overseas work carries political, currency and jurisdictional exposure, giving unanticipated delays, cost escalation and translation effects on earnings. Mitigation is assessing country risk before entering a market, operating through in-country entities and joint ventures, and hedging currency exposure where practical.
- Regulatory change mid-execution — Changes to regulation, safety legislation or environmental policy can alter project requirements mid-execution, causing delays, financial penalties or suspension of work; environmental and safety requirements continue to tighten. Mitigation is continuous tracking of regulatory developments, project-level compliance systems and early engagement with authorities on approvals.
- Skilled manpower availability and industrial relations — Skilled personnel are difficult to source in some trades and industrial relations can disrupt work, causing delays and quality shortfalls where crews are short. Mitigation is building a stable core workforce through training and progression, supplemented by planned outsourcing.
- Demand cyclicality in capital-intensive sectors — An economic slowdown may reduce the flow of new projects, particularly in capital-intensive sectors, reducing revenue and work in hand. Mitigation is diversifying across sectors and geographies so no single demand cycle governs the order book, and maintaining a recurring services layer that is less sensitive to the investment cycle.
bull_bear.title: Bear — key risks

business.body:
- **Power (57% Q4 / 64% FY26 of revenue)** — installation/erection, civil, structural, O&M, now BOP EPC.
- **Non-power (43% Q4 / 36% FY26)** — civil infra, railways, water, metro O&M, MDO.
- **MDO**: KBP mine (started Nov, 1.6mt FY26, INR 248 cr rev over 5 months; March alone INR 117 cr exceptional); SAIL/Tasra (INR 106 cr FY26, washery completing Dec-26, production from mid-Q4 FY27). EBITDA ~15% now → ~20% at peak rate capacity (KBP FY30, SAIL/Tasra FY29). Full-capacity revenue ~INR 2,100–2,200 cr (4mt SAIL + 5mt KBP). NOTE: FY28 MDO guide CUT from prior INR 1,800–1,900 cr to INR 1,250 cr (conservative ramp + CCL washery not ready).
- **Water division**: drag on margins. Order INR 2,700 cr, INR 1,800 cr executed, INR 900 cr balance (INR 700 cr to execute, INR 200 cr WIP). INR 90 cr receivable + INR 128 cr uncertified pending. Execution paused; shifting ~500 schemes to O&M (300+ done) for fixed monthly state revenue. Not taking new water work.

business.title: Positioning (investor deck)

business.body:
- [Margin drivers] Management attributes the margin decline to "an increase in royalty costs in the KRBM project following the Government Order on royalty sharing for seized quantities, higher OB removal costs at the KBP mine and increased material costs due to the ongoing middle east conflict" - the royalty change is a regulatory event, and the OB removal spend is described as "higher OB removal costs to make new seams accessible for future production and ramp-up".
- [Backlog composition] The order backlog breakup is overwhelmingly MDO (INR 39,330 Cr of INR 55,398 Cr on the chart's labelling), with the balance across Civil Infra, O&M, Industrial EPC and Industrial Construction; note the deck elsewhere sizes operationalized MDO contracts at INR 39,169 Cr, a different figure.
- [Backlog growth] Order backlog including MDO is shown as 23,027 / 57,053 / 53,994 / 55,151 / 55,398 for FY23 / FY24 / FY25 / FY26 / Q1FY27 - i.e. broadly flat since the MDO step-up in FY24, with annual order inflow of 8,479 / 8,314 / 6,347 / 7,210 across FY23-FY26.
- [Group structure] The leadership team includes whole-time directors for KTMPL, KBP Mining and PM Green Pvt. Ltd, indicating mining and green-energy activity is housed in separate entities; consolidated PAT carries a material non-controlling interest (INR 47.69 Cr in FY26 against INR 21.07 Cr in FY25).
- [Governance] The board is weighted with power-sector veterans - a non-executive director with 38+ years at BHEL and an independent director with 37+ years at BHEL including over 6 years as Chairman & MD, plus an independent director with 40+ years in Indian infrastructure.
business.title: Notable from the deck

business.body: Power Mech Projects erects, tests and commissions boilers, turbines, generators, critical piping and balance-of-plant systems for thermal and industrial plants, and has extended the same capability into repairs, overhauling, renovation and modernisation, long-term operation and maintenance, civil and structural construction, electrical transmission and distribution, mining development and operation, and turnkey balance-of-plant EPC. It is a business-to-business contractor serving government bodies, public sector undertakings, private enterprises and industrial organisations across India and select international markets in South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia. Work spans thermal, nuclear, hydro and renewable power, steel, refineries, cement and petrochemicals, roads, railways, metro, water and irrigation.
business.title: What they do

business.body:
- **Mechanical (erection and material handling):** Erection, testing and commissioning of boiler, turbine and generator, critical piping, electrostatic precipitators and auxiliaries, Coal handling plants including stackers, reclaimers, crushers, feeders, conveyors and silos, Ash handling in dense and lean phase configurations, Ore and bulk handling for iron ore, limestone, alumina and clinker, Overland and pipe conveyor systems, Industrial piping in carbon steel, stainless steel and alloy, In-house fabrication shop supporting live plant shutdown work
- **Infrastructure Construction:** Main plant civil including boiler foundations, bed plates, turbine generator decks, control room basements and structural columns, Balance of plant civil including cooling towers, pump houses, coal and ash handling civil, chimneys, switchyards and water systems, Structural steel supply, fabrication and erection, prefabricated erection, pipe racks and cable trenches, Nuclear civil covering containment auxiliary structures and balance of plant civil, Two, four and six-laning of National Highways, bridges and flyovers under Hybrid Annuity Model and EPC contracts, New Broad Gauge railway lines, doubling and quadrupling, Road Under Bridges, Road Over Bridges, wagon workshops, depots, yards and formation works, Metro depot-cum-workshops, stations and associated support structures, Government buildings, medical colleges and urban utility infrastructure, Canals, saddle dams and distribution networks on EPC and turnkey bases
- **Electrical, Transmission and Distribution:** Transmission lines and substations spanning 33 kV distribution to 400 kV transmission, Air-insulated and gas-insulated substations up to 400 kV with transformers, switchgear and control panels, High and low tension distribution lines, pole erection and distribution transformer installation, Supervisory control and data acquisition systems, ring main units, advanced metering and feeder automation, 25 kV overhead equipment, traction substations and signalling and telecommunication work for railway electrification
- **International Operations:** Shutdown management, Capital overhauls and repairs, Specialist manpower supply, Operation and maintenance of thermal, gas-fired and desalination assets
- **Industrial Services:** Long-term power plant operation and maintenance contracts across thermal, gas, nuclear and renewable assets, including coal handling, ash handling and water treatment systems, Industrial and process plant work in refineries, cement, steel and petrochemical facilities, spanning boilers, chillers, compressors and electrical and instrumentation systems, Turbine and generator overhauling, Urban mobility operation and maintenance for metro and monorail systems
- **EPC Division:** Turnkey balance of plant packages for thermal power projects, Cooling towers based on induced-draft and natural-draft technologies, Coal, biomass and ash handling systems, Pre-Treatment, Demineralization, Circulating Water, Effluent Treatment Plant and Sewage Treatment Plant water systems, Fire protection and detection systems, Air-conditioning and ventilation systems

outlook.body:
- **FY27 revenue: ~21% growth** (CFO explicitly confirmed it is revenue, not order growth). FY26 had targeted ~6,500 cr, achieved ~6,062; "actual shortfall only INR 438 cr" after offsetting water-division delays.
- **FY27 order inflow target: INR 12,000 cr** (FY28 range INR 12,000–15,000 cr). Opportunity basket tracked: ~INR 70,000 cr; bids ~INR 40,000–50,000 cr; historical hit ratio ~15%.
- **FY27 EBITDA: ~12.5% (incl other income), +0.25–0.3%** vs 12.3%. Long-term: +~0.5%/yr to ~14% by FY30, ~14.25% FY31.
- **MDO FY27: INR 500 cr** (KBP INR 350 cr + SAIL/Tasra INR 150 cr); FY28 INR 1,250 cr (KBP 500 + Tasra 750). MDO mix 7% of revenue FY27 → 13% FY28.

outlook.body:
- Total backlog INR 55,151 cr incl MDO; ex-MDO executable INR 15,899 cr. Power ~70% / non-power ~30% of backlog. Average order tenure 2.5 yrs; ~40% of opening OB executed each year.
- Power opportunity: ordering on BHEL/L&T packages ~INR 2.8 lakh cr → addressable for Power Mech ~INR 60,000 cr (installation, civil, structural, BOP).
- Client concentration: Adani 6,400 MW / ~INR 3,166–3,200 cr ongoing; BHEL 7,000 MW thermal + 1,400 MW nuclear; with Singareni BOP (INR 2,550 cr) total BHEL packages ~INR 4,700 cr.

outlook.title: Growth verticals / optionality

outlook.body:
- Enter a new vertical only when it draws on a capability the Company already holds, so that each new business deepens execution rather than diluting it
- Move from executing individual packages under a lead contractor to owning complete turnkey systems, anchored by the entry into large-format Balance of Plant EPC through the Singareni package for BHEL
- Keep the operation and maintenance franchise, described as already the largest in the country, as the anchor of the business
- Convert the two mining contracts, which moved into execution during FY 2025-26, into a scaled business drawing on the same civil and material-handling strengths
- Keep the international business concentrated in operation and maintenance and manpower services rather than construction, which kept the Company largely insulated from disruption in West Asia and delivers steady, annuity-like returns
- Operate through eight strategic business units that each sit inside a national requirement for reliable power, durable infrastructure and domestically secured resources
- Build out renewable and solar exposure through dedicated subsidiaries: PM Green Private Limited for solar and other renewable energy opportunities, and Suryatna Projects Private Limited for solar projects under the PM Kusum scheme in Bihar, covering solar pump installation, solarisation of agricultural pumps and small solar plants on barren land
- Develop a software capability through PMTS Private Limited and its step-down subsidiaries PMTS Technology LLC in Dubai and PMTS Inc. in the United States
- Expand the Noida workshop of Power Mech Industri Private Limited in line with the need in the industry
- Grow the hydro business through Hydro Magus Private Limited, which the Directors' Report describes as fully geared and aggressively planning for undertaking comprehensive projects in India and neighbouring countries
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Expansion in FY 2025-26 was in footprint, entity structure and contract scope rather than in disclosed rupee capex. The Company incorporated into Balance of Plant EPC with the package for the 1 x 800 MW Singareni thermal power project for BHEL, which the Chairman describes as moving the Company from executing individual packages to owning complete turnkey systems. Both Mine Developer and Operator mandates entered execution, with production under way at Kotre Basantpur Pachmo and washery construction progressing at Tasra; the mining subsidiaries named in the Directors' Report are KBP Mining Private Limited, incorporated for the exploration, design, engineering, development and operation of mines, and Kalyaneswari Tasra Mining Private Limited, incorporated for exploring, design and engineering, developing, operating and working at the Tasra open cast mine in Jharkhand, alongside Kailash River Bed Minerals LLP, Vindyavasini Mining Works LLP, Vanshika Mining Works LLP and Velocity Mining Works LLP. Four new subsidiaries were incorporated during the year: PM Green Private Limited (D.O.I: 09-04-2025) for exploring opportunities in solar and other renewable energy projects, Deoghar Ring Road Project Private Limited (D.O.I: 02-05-2025) to execute a 4 lane bypass to NH-114A connecting NH-333 and NH-133 in Jharkhand over 49.00 km on Hybrid Annuity mode, PMTS Inc., USA (D.O.I: 24-06-2025), and Suryatna Projects Private Limited (D.O.I: 16-07-2025). The manufacturing footprint is the Noida workshop of wholly-owned subsidiary Power Mech Industri Private Limited, where the Directors' Report states the machines are working at full steam and further expansion is proceeding in line with the need in the industry. Geographic footprint per BRSR Section A is 20 offices nationally and 3 internationally with no plants reported, serving 20 states and 7 countries; the international business contributed 5% of revenue in FY 2025-26, spanning South Asia, the Middle East, Africa and Central Asia, having shifted from large-scale erection projects towards O&M services and skilled manpower deployment, which the Company says requires lower working capital and provides stronger margins and greater earnings stability. The demand backdrop cited for this expansion is the Union Government capital expenditure allocation of Rs 11.21 lakh crore for FY 2025-26, coal-based capacity rising from 228 GW in FY 2025-26 to 291 GW by 2031-32, storage rising from about 6 GW to 81 GW by 2031-32, and nuclear opening to regulated private participation under the SHANTI Act, 2025. No rupee capital-expenditure or capital-commitment quantum is usable from this bundle: the two capital commitments disclosure blocks supplied carry no attributable figure or printed unit.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- Coal-based capacity is being augmented from 228 GW in FY 2025-26 to 291 GW by 2031-32, an addition of about 63 GW over six years, reflecting a deliberate near-term emphasis on base-load capacity to balance generation as solar and wind expand
- Record generation capacity addition of 57.53 GW during FY 2025-26 against 33.24 GW in FY 2024-25, with total installed capacity at 532.74 GW as on 31 March 2026 and non-fossil sources at 53.2% or 283.47 GW
- The SHANTI Act, 2025, which received Presidential assent in December 2025, replaces the Atomic Energy Act, 1962 and the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010 and opens nuclear development to regulated private participation for the first time, with consequences running across several of the Company's businesses
- Government projects nuclear capacity of over 22 GW by the early 2030s as indigenous 700 MW and 1,000 MW reactors come on line, and the Nuclear Energy Mission targets 100 GW by 2047
- Energy storage build-out: the Central Electricity Authority estimates storage capacity must rise from about 6 GW today to 81 GW by 2031-32, comprising about 44 GW of pumped storage and 37 GW of battery storage
- The changing generation mix works in favour of engineering, project execution and service companies, because planned additions across coal, pumped storage, battery storage and nuclear all translate into construction and service scope
- Transmission expansion in step with generation: the national network has exceeded 5 lakh circuit kilometres with total transformation capacity of 1,407 GVA, the National Electricity Plan is finalised with estimated investment of Rs 9.15 lakh crore against projected peak demand of 388 GW by 2032, and energy requirement is expected to rise from 1,929 billion units in FY 2026-27 to 3,366 billion units by 2035-36
- Union Government capital expenditure allocation of Rs 11.21 lakh crore for FY 2025-26 directed at roads, railways, urban infrastructure, power, energy and minerals, carrying forward the National Infrastructure Pipeline and National Monetisation Pipeline, widening the addressable opportunity for engineering and construction contractors
- The Electricity (Amendment) Rules, 2026 clarified captive generating plant ownership and consumption thresholds and recognised group structures, reducing regulatory risk for the steel, aluminium, cement and chemicals industries; the installed captive base is nearly 81 GW in units ranging from 1 MW to 600 MW
- The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy targets 566 GW of installed non-fossil capacity by 2031-32, and India met its 50% non-fossil installed capacity target five years ahead of its 2030 Nationally Determined Contribution commitment
- India's real GDP grew 7.7% in FY 2025-26 and is projected at a stable 6.9% in FY 2026-27 on domestic consumption and the public capital expenditure cycle, with the Reserve Bank easing the repo rate from 6.25% to 5.25% over the year
- Margin headwind called out by the Chairman: margins came under some pressure in the water division, where certification of completed work by the state remained delayed through the year, offset by strong execution across the core power and O&M strategic business units
- Foreign exchange earnings for the year rose to Rs 318 Cr from Rs 235 Cr, with the long-standing presence across the Middle East and West Africa continuing to deliver steady, annuity-like returns
- Risks to the outlook flagged in the MD&A: rising global energy prices and supply-chain disruption arising from the conflicts in West Asia and Ukraine could add to inflationary pressure and weigh on growth, and wider involvement of global powers in either conflict would compound the trade and logistics impact
- Order backlog, including long-tenure mining contracts, closed the year at Rs 55,151 Cr, giving multi-year visibility into the business ahead

risks.note: A significant share of revenue is drawn from a limited number of large clients and government entities, so a material reduction in their capital programmes would affect revenue disproportionately. Listed both as a Threat and in the risk management table; mitigation is to broaden the client base across private enterprises and new sectors and to lengthen contract tenors so revenue is less dependent on annual award cycles.

Receivables can remain outstanding where budgetary allocation to a government-funded programme is delayed, holding up certification and collection. The AR states this has been a feature of the water business during the year, and the Chairman attributes margin pressure in the water division to certification of completed work by the state remaining delayed through the year.
risks.risk: Delays in government fund allocation holding up certification and collection

risks.note: The construction and maintenance sector has a large number of participants of varying scale, domestic and international, offering comparable services; this can intensify competition, compress margins and lower the probability of conversion on competitively bid work. Mitigation is long-term client relationships, specialised services where the field is narrower, and selective bidding rather than bidding on volume.

Prices of steel, cement and other inputs fluctuate and delivery of manufactured items can slip, with geopolitical disruption able to move prices sharply, giving higher project cost and margin erosion on fixed-price work. Mitigation is contracts incorporating price adjustment clauses, long-term supply arrangements and hedging where instruments are available.
risks.risk: Input cost and supply chain exposure on fixed-price work

risks.note: Weather, site access, land availability and clearance delays can disrupt execution, producing schedule slippage, cost escalation and exposure to liquidated damages. Mitigation is planning with contingency, project controls and scheduling systems, and holding safety and quality standards across sites.

Heavy machinery, working at height and live plant environments carry inherent safety risk; an incident or compliance failure can give rise to injury, legal consequence, contractual penalty and reputational damage. Mitigation is safety management systems, training and audit at every site, with incident reporting and corrective action tracked to closure.
risks.risk: Safety and reputational exposure on heavy-machinery and live-plant work

risks.note: Overseas work carries political, currency and jurisdictional exposure, giving unanticipated delays, cost escalation and translation effects on earnings. Mitigation is assessing country risk before entering a market, operating through in-country entities and joint ventures, and hedging currency exposure where practical.
risks.risk: International operations: political, currency and jurisdictional exposure

risks.note: Changes to regulation, safety legislation or environmental policy can alter project requirements mid-execution, causing delays, financial penalties or suspension of work; environmental and safety requirements continue to tighten. Mitigation is continuous tracking of regulatory developments, project-level compliance systems and early engagement with authorities on approvals.
